overview.title: Noise channels cost accuracy; feature selection
overview.section: 5.1 Generalization: The goal of machine learning
overview.main_topic: Result of the noise-channel experiment (figure 5.6) and feature selection as a remedy for noisy features.
overview.central_idea: Although both datasets contain the same information, the model trained with noise channels ends about one percentage point lower in validation accuracy, purely because of spurious correlations. When unsure whether features are informative, select features by a usefulness score such as mutual information with the labels.
overview.importance: It delivers the empirical evidence for the claim that noisy features inevitably cause overfitting, and introduces feature selection, a practical tool that links back to the IMDB vocabulary cut-off.

summary:
The page opens with the end of **Listing 5.3**: the second `plt.plot` call draws the zeros-channel validation accuracy as a red dashed line (`"r--"`), then the figure gets a title ("Effect of noise channels on validation accuracy"), axis labels ("Epochs", "Accuracy"), integer x-ticks (`plt.xticks(epochs)`) and a legend before `plt.show()`.

**The result (figure 5.6).** The zeros-channel model (red dashed) starts around 0.954 after epoch 1 and plateaus near 0.977. The noise-channel model (blue solid) starts much lower, around 0.911, climbs unevenly (dipping at epochs 4 and 9) and ends near 0.965. The book summarizes: despite the data holding the same information, the noise model ends **about one percentage point lower**, purely through spurious correlations, and **the more noise channels you add, the further accuracy would degrade**.

**Remedy: feature selection.** "Noisy features inevitably lead to overfitting." So when you are not sure whether your features are informative or distracting, it is common to do **feature selection** before training. Restricting IMDB to the 10,000 most common words (chapter 4) was a crude form of it. The typical method is to compute a **usefulness score** for each feature, a measure of how informative it is about the task, such as the **mutual information** between the feature and the labels, and keep only features above a threshold. Applied to this experiment, it would filter out the white-noise channels, which have (near-)zero mutual information with the digit labels.

This closes subsection 5.1.1; the next page starts 5.1.2 on why deep learning generalizes at all.

paragraphs.what_it_says: Although both datasets hold the same information, validation accuracy with noise channels ends about one percentage point lower, purely through spurious correlations (figure 5.6). More noise channels would degrade accuracy further.

paragraphs.what_it_means: Instead of hoping the model ignores useless inputs, remove them before training. concepts.name: Feature selection
concepts.definition: Keeping only input features judged informative for the task, typically by computing a usefulness score per feature and thresholding it.
concepts.intuition: Before studying, throw out the pages of static so you can't 'learn' from them.
concepts.technical: Filter methods score features independently of the model (mutual information, chi-squared, correlation, frequency); the top-k or above-threshold features are kept.
concepts.significance: The book's remedy for noisy features; it would remove the noise channels in Listing 5.1.
concepts.example: Keeping the 10,000 most common IMDB words; dropping features with near-zero mutual information with the labels.
concepts.misconception: Frequency-based cuts are not the same as informativeness: a frequent word like 'the' is common but carries little sentiment information.

concepts.name: Mutual information
concepts.definition: A measure of how much knowing one variable reduces uncertainty about another; named in the book as a usefulness score between a feature and the labels.
concepts.intuition: How many yes/no questions about the label you save by looking at the feature.
concepts.technical: I(X;Y) = H(Y) − H(Y|X) ≥ 0, with equality iff X and Y are independent. Captures nonlinear dependence, unlike correlation.
concepts.significance: A principled way to rank features for selection.
concepts.example: A pixel in the centre of MNIST images has positive MI with the digit; a white-noise column has MI ≈ 0.
concepts.misconception: Low MI of a single feature doesn't always mean it's useless: features can be informative only in combination (e.g. XOR). Filter methods miss such interactions.

concepts.name: Spurious correlation
concepts.definition: A chance association between a feature and the target in the training sample that doesn't hold in general.
concepts.technical: Figure 5.6 measures its cost: about one percentage point of validation accuracy on MNIST with 784 noise channels.
concepts.significance: The book attributes the accuracy gap 'purely' to it.
concepts.example: The noise-channel model's lower curve in figure 5.6.
concepts.misconception: 'The model will learn to ignore noise.' It partially does, but not before fitting some of it.

math.title: Mutual information between a feature and the labels
math.latex: I(X_j; Y) = \sum_{x,\,y} p(x, y)\,\log\frac{p(x, y)}{p(x)\,p(y)} = H(Y) - H(Y\mid X_j)
math.source_text: Named in words only: 'the mutual information between the feature and the labels'. The formula is not printed in the book.

variables.meaning: Feature j (e.g. one pixel or noise column, discretized).
Joint probability of feature value x and label y.
Remaining uncertainty about the label after observing feature j.

math.operations: Sum over all value pairs of the joint probability times the log-ratio of joint to product of marginals.
math.purpose: Serves as the per-feature usefulness score for threshold-based feature selection.
math.interpretation: Zero if the feature is independent of the label (p(x,y) = p(x)p(y)); larger values mean the feature is more informative.
math.intuition: If knowing the feature never changes your guess about the label, it shares no information with it.
math.numerical_example: Binary label with H(Y) = 1 bit. A white-noise feature leaves H(Y|X) = 1 bit → I = 0. A feature that perfectly determines the label gives H(Y|X) = 0 → I = 1 bit. In practice, MI estimated from finite data is slightly positive even for noise, which is why a threshold is used.

deeper.title: Reading figure 5.6 carefully
deeper.body:
Values read from the plot (approximate):

| epoch | zeros (red dashed) | noise (blue solid) | gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.954 | 0.911 | 0.043 |
| 3 | 0.973 | 0.950 | 0.023 |
| 6 | 0.977 | 0.962 | 0.015 |
| 10 | 0.977 | 0.965 | 0.012 |

The gap shrinks over training but persists at roughly 1-1.5 points, consistent with the book's 'about one percentage point'. In error-rate terms, 2.3% vs. 3.5% means the noise model makes about 50% more mistakes. Beyond the book: the early gap also reflects slower optimization, since gradients from noise columns perturb the hidden layer, not only overfitting.

deeper.title: Feature selection in practice
deeper.body: Note (not in the book): scikit-learn provides `mutual_info_classif` and `SelectKBest` for exactly the score-and-threshold approach described. Applied to the 1,568-column noise dataset, the 784 noise columns would receive near-zero scores and be dropped, as the book says. Note that some real MNIST pixels (corners, always 0) would also be dropped, which is harmless. For deep learning on raw signals (images, audio), explicit feature selection is less common because architectures like convnets impose their own priors; it remains common for tabular data.

deeper.title: Radio static analogy
deeper.body: Listening to a station with static mixed in, you can still understand the song, but occasionally you 'hear' words that are really crackle. Turning down the static channel (feature selection) is easier than training yourself to ignore it.

questions.question: According to figure 5.6 and the text, how much lower does the noise-channel model's validation accuracy end up?
questions.explanation: The text says 'about one percentage point lower'; the plot ends near 0.965 vs. 0.977. The other options contradict the figure.

questions.question: Why does the book say the drop is 'purely' due to spurious correlations?
questions.answer: Because the experiment holds everything else fixed: same model, training settings and information content. The only difference is whether the extra columns vary randomly (and can be fit by chance) or are constant zeros.
questions.explanation: This is the controlled design of Listings 5.1-5.2 (pp.164-165).

questions.question: Describe the typical feature selection procedure the book outlines.
questions.answer: Compute a usefulness score for each feature, a measure of how informative it is for the task such as its mutual information with the labels, and keep only the features whose score exceeds a threshold.
questions.explanation: Stated in the last paragraph; the book notes this would remove the white-noise channels.

questions.question: Which earlier preprocessing step does the book call 'a crude form of feature selection'?
options: Restricting IMDB data to the top 10,000 most common words
questions.answer: Restricting IMDB data to the top 10,000 most common words
questions.explanation: Quoted directly. Scaling and one-hot encoding transform features without removing any; validation_split selects samples, not features.

questions.question: A binary label has entropy H(Y) = 1 bit. Feature A leaves H(Y|A) = 1 bit; feature B leaves H(Y|B) = 0.4 bits. Compute the mutual information of each with the label. Which would a threshold of 0.1 bits keep?
questions.answer: I(A;Y) = 0 bits, I(B;Y) = 0.6 bits; only B is kept.
questions.explanation: I(X;Y) = H(Y) − H(Y|X). Feature A behaves like a white-noise channel (formula added beyond the book).

questions.question: In Listing 5.3, what do "r--" and plt.xticks(epochs) do?
questions.answer: "r--" draws the zeros curve as a red dashed line; plt.xticks(epochs) puts x-axis ticks at each integer epoch 1-10.
questions.explanation: Standard matplotlib format string and tick control, matching figure 5.6's appearance.

questions.question: Can you predict what figure 5.6 would look like with 3 × 784 noise channels instead of 784, and justify it?
questions.answer: The noise curve would sit even lower, with a larger gap to the zeros curve, because there are more varying meaningless features to find chance correlations in.
questions.explanation: The book states 'The more noise channels you might add, the further accuracy would degrade.'
